title: Robust and leakage-resilient device-independent oblivious transfer in MiniQCryp
authors: Zhili Chen, Rahul Jain, YaoNan Zhang
abstract: Assuming post-quantum one-way functions, we construct device-independent (DI) oblivious transfer (OT) and bit commitment: honest parties use only trusted classical computation to operate untrusted quantum devices, which may share arbitrary entanglement and behave non-IID. Security is simulation-based against quantum polynomial-time adversaries and composes sequentially with efficient simulators. One protocol skeleton serves both, in two regimes. With isolated laboratories and coordinate-local measurements in the honest receiver's device, it tolerates a constant rate of honest-device faults. With polylogarithmically many qubits of adaptive leakage between the laboratories and arbitrary joint measurements, it tolerates an inverse-polylogarithmic rate. Each elementary DI call uses a fresh, isolated batch of polylogarithmically many device coordinates, and total device use in the compiled OT protocol is polynomial. The commitment has efficient simulators against both parties and yields DI coin tossing with abort.   Because OT is complete for secure computation, the construction yields a DI protocol, with abort, for every efficiently computable classical functionality on a fixed number of parties, secure against static corruption of any proper subset of them.   The commitment's extractor changes a public parity relation through classical equivocation and leaves the device execution, hence its leakage, unchanged. A commit-and-prove functionality, disjoint audits, and an affine consistency check link the certified correlations to ideal OT. Sender security rests on a selector-aware parallel-repetition bound for the Magic Square game, which we derive from the two-round threshold theorem of Kundu and Tan.
summary: This work presents device-independent protocols for oblivious transfer and bit commitment, ensuring security even when the quantum devices are untrusted and potentially faulty. It achieves robustness by explicitly accounting for information leakage and device faults in two distinct operational regimes. This advances the practical feasibility of quantum cryptography by providing concrete, resilient cryptographic primitives.
main_problem: The paper addresses the construction of robust and leakage-resilient device-independent (DI) oblivious transfer (OT) and bit commitment (BC) protocols.
main_result: It successfully constructs DI OT and BC protocols secure against quantum polynomial-time adversaries, which are robust to certain levels of device faults and information leakage.
method: The construction relies on a chain of reductions involving a commit-and-prove functionality, utilizing techniques like selector-aware parallel-repetition bounds and classical equivocation.
model_or_system: The security is based on observed correlations from the Magic Square game using untrusted quantum devices in two laboratories, rather than assuming perfect device behavior.
key_observables: Fault rates (constant or inverse-polylogarithmic), information leakage ($\ell$ qubits), and the security parameter ($\lambda$).
important_parameters: The protocols are analyzed in two regimes: isolated laboratories with coordinate-local measurements, or general settings allowing adaptive leakage.
main_assumptions: The primary assumptions are the existence of post-quantum one-way functions (qOWFs) and the ability to use fresh, isolated batches of device coordinates.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the reduction chains, comparing the new work to prior protocols by highlighting the removal of trusted quantum operations and the requirement for bounded leakage.
paper_structure: The paper develops the security proof by building upon existing DI protocols, detailing the reduction from OT to general secure computation, and providing specific analyses for the commitment and coin tossing functionalities.
why_interesting: While highly theoretical, the focus on device-independent security and fault tolerance is crucial for realizing quantum technologies in noisy, real-world physical systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Reduction chains. The two earlier chains use trusted quantum communication and place no condition on devices; “weak” permits inefficient simulation, vCDS is verifiable conditional disclosure of secrets, and the chain of [BCKM21] also runs from EFI pairs [BCQ23], which need that quantum communication. Ours removes the trusted quantum operations; in exchange, its two DI arrows require fresh isolated batches with bounded leakage (fresh isolated batches, bounded leakage). Its boxes name the protocol and the section that proves each step; the middle arrow is classical outside its BC calls, OT completeness gives MPC, and the commitment also yields coin tossing (Section 5.5).
